questions.q: In Financial Services Cloud, what replaces the standard sales-object focus of a generic Salesforce org?
options: A completely custom object model with no standard objects at all
Financial Accounts, Financial Holdings, and client relationship objects built around the client's actual financial life
Opportunities and Products, unchanged from a standard org
Cases and Entitlements, since FSC is built on the Service Cloud data model
questions.explain: FSC reshapes the data model around what a client owns and who they're related to, rather than sales pipeline objects — missing this leads an architect to duplicate or ignore the existing model.

questions.q: Why can't every sensitive field use the strongest available Shield Platform Encryption scheme without consequence?
options: Shield only supports encrypting one field per object
Encryption schemes in Shield cannot be mixed within the same org
The strongest non-deterministic schemes can't be used in report filters, list-view sorts, or similar operations, so a field the business needs to query on may need a different scheme
Stronger encryption always slows down every API call regardless of the field
questions.explain: The real trade-off is searchability versus protection strength — the strongest scheme can break filtering/sorting, which is why the design matches the scheme to how each specific field actually needs to be used.

questions.q: Where does the exposure-threshold segregation-of-duties rule (no single RM approves above a set amount alone) belong in the design?
options: In a training document telling RMs not to approve large accounts themselves
Nowhere specific — it's assumed RMs will self-police
In a validation rule that simply blocks all approvals above the threshold permanently
In the record's approval process, with the second-approver requirement enforced by the approval step's logic rather than left to individual judgment
questions.explain: A segregation-of-duties control has to be enforced structurally in the approval process, not left as an informal expectation, or it isn't actually a control.

questions.q: Why is the KYC/AML vendor call made through a Named Credential rather than embedding the vendor's API key directly in Apex or Flow?
options: It centralizes the vendor's authentication details in one configuration, keeps secrets out of code, and lets the endpoint or key change without a code deployment
Named Credentials make the call faster than any other method
Named Credentials are required by every third-party vendor's contract
It is the only way Flow is able to make an HTTP callout at all
questions.explain: The architectural benefit is centralized, changeable, secret-free configuration — not raw speed and not a contractual requirement.

questions.q: Why does the prospect-facing Experience Cloud portal represent a different trust boundary from the bank's internal FSC org?
options: Because Experience Cloud and FSC cannot technically be deployed in the same org
Because Experience Cloud users automatically get the same access as internal RMs
Because external prospect users authenticate with access scoped only to their own in-progress application, never to another client's data or internal records
Because the portal has no identity or authentication model at all
questions.explain: The portal's external identity is deliberately scoped tightly to the prospect's own data — that scoping is exactly what keeps a compromised or malicious prospect session from reaching anyone else's records.
